burn.title: Where the tokens go
burn.lead: Every API call re-sends the whole conversation. So the cost of a tool result, a skill's instructions or an MCP response is not only its size once (ingest) — it is re-read on every later call of the session until the context is compacted (carry). This page attributes {attributed} of {total} ({pct}) to what put tokens into the context; the rest is rounding in the calibration. Sizes are calibrated per call against the real cache-write counts the API reported.
burn.heavyLead: One big result early in a long session is the classic token burner: it is re-read on every following call.
burn.longLead: Sessions whose average context was ≥ 100k tokens. Their cost is dominated by re-reading context.
burn.missesLead: Each miss re-processed the whole context at the cache-write rate.
burn.catHint: {cat}: ingest {ingest} · carry {carry} · output {out} · {tokens} tokens put into context
save.title: How to reduce cost / stay under the limits
save.lead: Findings computed from your own transcripts in the selected range ({cost} across {n} sessions), followed by the general guideline. On a Pro/Max plan the dollar figures are notional, but plan limits (the 5-hour session window and the weekly cap) are consumed by the same tokens, so the same levers apply.
f.long.title: {pct} of your spend is re-reading context (cache reads)
f.long.body: Every API call re-sends the whole conversation. {detail} With a 1M context window a session can grow to 400–500k tokens, and then even a one-line question costs ~$0.25 just to re-read the history.
f.long.detail: Your {n} longest-context sessions alone spent {cr} of their {cost} on cache reads (average context {ctx} tokens in "{title}").
f.long.tip1: /clear when you switch to an unrelated task (use /rename first so you can /resume it later).
f.long.tip2: /compact at natural breaks — before the context gets huge, not when auto-compact forces it mid-task. Add focus: /compact keep the API design and the failing test.
f.long.tip3: Watch the context in the status line or with /context; treat 150k+ as a signal to compact.
f.long.tip4: Use /rewind instead of continuing after a wrong turn — it truncates to a still-cached prefix.
f.miss.title: {n} cache misses re-processed the full context
f.miss.body: A miss happens when the cached prefix is gone: idle longer than the cache TTL (1 hour on a subscription within plan usage, 5 minutes on API key / usage credits / subagents), a model or effort switch (/model was used {model}×), fast mode, or a Claude Code upgrade. Worst session: "{title}" with {misses} misses ≈ {cost}.
f.miss.tip1: Pick model and effort at the start of a session, not in the middle.
f.miss.tip2: Coming back after a long break to a big session? Accept the "resume from summary" offer, or /clear and start fresh instead of paying to rebuild 400k tokens of cache.
f.miss.tip3: On an API key: "promptCacheTtl": "1h" in settings.json keeps the cache warm through longer breaks (cache writes cost 2× instead of 1.25×, but a rebuild costs far more).
f.miss.tip4: Subagents always get the 5-minute TTL unless you set subagentPromptCacheTtl.
f.model.title: Opus is {pct} of spend — the same tokens on Sonnet would have cost {son} instead of {cur}
f.model.body: Sonnet 5 is 2.5× cheaper per token and handles most implementation work. Reserve Opus for architecture, hard debugging and planning. Your default model setting is {model}.
f.model.tip1: /model sonnet for routine coding sessions; switch at the start (a mid-session switch is a cache miss).
f.model.tip2: Give subagents a cheaper model: model: haiku or sonnet in the agent frontmatter, or ask for "use sonnet for the subagents".
f.model.tip3: Lower effort on the big model is often cheaper than a model cascade — see the effort finding.
f.think.title: {pct} of output tokens are thinking
f.think.body: {n} thinking tokens, billed as output (the most expensive kind). Effort levels seen: {efforts}. Thinking is worth it for planning and debugging; it is wasted on "rename this", "run the tests", "commit".
f.think.tip1: /effort low (or medium) for simple, mechanical sessions; keep high/xhigh for design and hard bugs.
f.think.tip2: Set it at session start — changing effort mid-session invalidates the cache on most models.
f.think.tip3: The impact figure assumes about half of the thinking could be avoided (at Opus output price).
f.shell.title: Shell output is your biggest context burner: {cost} ({pct})
f.shell.body: {n} shell commands put {tokens} tokens of output into context ({per} per command on average), and {carry} of the cost is that output being re-read afterwards. Test runners, build logs, git log, ls -R and cat of big files are the usual culprits.
f.shell.tip1: Ask for filtered output: "run the tests and show only failures" — or add a PreToolUse hook that pipes test/build commands through grep -E "FAIL|ERROR" | head -100 (example in the Claude Code cost docs).
f.shell.tip2: Delegate verbose operations to a subagent ("run the full test suite in a subagent and report only failures") — the noise stays in the subagent's context.
f.shell.tip3: Prefer head, tail, --quiet flags; avoid cat-ing whole files when a grep would do.
f.shell.tip4: The impact figure assumes half of the carried output could have been filtered away.
f.files.title: Reading and writing files: {cost} ({pct})
f.files.body: Reads put {rd} tokens into context, edits/writes {ed} (the file content the model writes is output and stays in the context afterwards). Heaviest single read in range: {max} tokens.
f.files.tip1: Point Claude at the exact file/function ("in auth.ts, the login function") — vague asks like "improve the codebase" trigger broad scanning.
f.files.tip2: Install a code-intelligence (LSP) plugin for your languages: "go to definition" replaces grep + reading several candidate files.
f.files.tip3: Large generated files, lockfiles and data dumps: tell Claude not to read them, or keep them out of the repo it explores.
f.files.tip4: Prefer Edit (a diff) over rewriting whole files with Write — a full rewrite costs the whole file in output tokens and again in context.
f.startup.title: Sessions start with {n} tokens before you type anything
f.startup.body: System prompt, tool definitions, CLAUDE.md, MCP server instructions and the skill listing are loaded on every session and re-read on every call ({cost} in range). Projects with the largest startup context: {projects}.
f.startup.tip1: Keep CLAUDE.md under ~200 lines; move workflow-specific instructions into skills (loaded only when invoked).
f.startup.tip2: /mcp — disable servers you are not using in this project; each adds instructions to every session.
f.startup.tip3: /context shows exactly what is in the window at startup.
f.startupOk.title: Startup context is lean ({n} tokens on average)
f.startupOk.body: System prompt + CLAUDE.md + MCP instructions cost {cost} in range — not your problem. Keep CLAUDE.md short and MCP servers deferred.
f.skills.title: What skills and MCP servers cost you
f.skills.tip1: A skill's instructions are injected into the context when invoked and re-read on every later call — a 40k-token skill in a 300-call session is ~12M cache-read tokens. Invoke heavy skills in a fresh or forked context, or split them.
f.skills.tip2: MCP results (page reads, screenshots) are big; prefer a CLI tool (gh, curl) when one exists, and text extraction / filtered reads over full page dumps.
f.skills.tip3: Browser screenshots count ~1.5k tokens each and Claude Code drops old ones in batches, which itself invalidates part of the cache.
f.sub.title: Subagents & workflows: {cost} ({pct})
f.sub.body: {list}. Subagents are the right tool for verbose work (their context is thrown away), but each one starts cold: its own system prompt, a 5-minute cache TTL, and your spawn prompt from scratch. Workflows fan out many agents at once.
f.sub.tip1: Keep spawn prompts focused and small; everything in them is paid per agent.
f.sub.tip2: Use Sonnet/Haiku for worker agents; reserve Opus for the orchestrator.
f.sub.tip3: Keep the number of parallel agents small — token usage is roughly proportional to the count.
f.retention.title: Claude Code deletes transcripts after {days} days (cleanupPeriodDays)
f.retention.body: Your stats cache says you started on {first}, but transcripts only exist from {firstTx} — earlier sessions were cleaned up (last cleanup {last}). This dashboard now keeps parsed data of deleted transcripts in its own cache (marked {archived}), but to keep the raw files raise the retention:
f.retention.tip1: Use the button below (or add "cleanupPeriodDays": 365 to ~/.claude/settings.json yourself).
guide.title: The guideline (from the Claude Code docs, condensed)
guide.html:
1. Understand what you pay for

Token cost scales with context size × number of calls. Claude Code re-sends the whole conversation on every API call; prompt caching makes the re-read cheap (≈10% of input price) but never free. Anthropic's own numbers: the average is about $13 per developer per active day, and 90% of users stay under $30/day. Your average in range is {perDay}/active day.

2. Manage context proactively

  • /clear between unrelated tasks; /rename + /resume to come back later.
  • /compact at natural breaks, with instructions on what to keep; or put a # Compact instructions section in CLAUDE.md.
  • /context and /usage show what is in the window and what counts against your plan (on subscriptions /usage also attributes recent usage to skills, subagents, plugins and MCP servers, and flags long context / cache misses).
  • /rewind (double Esc) to go back to a checkpoint instead of continuing down a wrong path.

3. Choose model and effort per task — at the start

  • Sonnet for most coding, Opus for architecture and hard reasoning, Haiku for trivial subagent tasks (model: haiku in the agent file).
  • /effort low|medium|high|xhigh|max; thinking tokens are billed as output. Switching model or effort mid-session throws away the cache on most models.

4. Keep the cache warm

  • Subscription within plan usage: 1-hour TTL for the main conversation. API key, usage credits and all subagents: 5 minutes. promptCacheTtl / subagentPromptCacheTtl ("5m" or "1h") or env CLAUDE_CODE_PROMPT_CACHE_TTL override it.
  • Things that invalidate the cache: model switch, effort change, fast mode on, MCP server connect/disconnect (when tools are not deferred), plugin toggles, denying a whole tool, compaction, dropping old images, upgrading Claude Code.
  • Things that are cache-safe: editing files, editing CLAUDE.md mid-session (does not apply until /clear), permission mode, output style, invoking skills, /rewind, spawning subagents.

5. Shrink what enters the context

  • Specific prompts ("add validation to login() in auth.ts") instead of "improve this".
  • Hooks that pre-filter tool output (test runners → failures only). Skills that describe the codebase so Claude does not explore it every time.
  • CLAUDE.md ≤ 200 lines; workflow instructions belong in skills. Disable unused MCP servers with /mcp; prefer CLIs (gh, aws, gcloud).
  • Code-intelligence plugins (LSP) for typed languages: precise navigation instead of grep + reading candidates.
  • Delegate verbose work (tests, docs fetching, log processing) to subagents; only the summary comes back.

6. Work in a way that avoids re-work

  • Plan mode (Shift+Tab) for complex tasks; approve the approach before implementation.
  • Give verification targets (tests, expected output, screenshots) so Claude can check itself.
  • Test incrementally; press Esc early when it heads the wrong way.

7. Background usage to know about

  • Session summaries for --resume, title generation and /usage checks cost a little (Haiku).
  • Scheduled tasks (/loop), cross-session messages and goal check-ins each send the full context when they fire — in a big session that is expensive while you are away.
  • Agent teams use roughly 7× the tokens of a normal session.

8. On a subscription: what "session limit" means

Pro/Max/Team seats have a rolling 5-hour window and a weekly cap shared across all models (plus model-specific caps). When you hit the session or weekly limit, switching models does not help; /usage-credits lets you continue on pay-as-you-go, and from v2.1.234 Claude Code can wait and auto-continue after the reset (/rate-limit-options). The same tokens that cost dollars on the API consume these windows — long context and cache misses are what burn them fastest.

Sources

  • Manage costs effectively — Claude Code docs
  • How Claude Code uses prompt caching
  • Explore the context window, Subagents, The ~/.claude directory
  • API pricing
lt.title: Lifetime, from Claude Code's own stats cache
lt.lead: Claude Code keeps its own counters in stats-cache.json since your very first session — including the days whose transcripts it has already deleted. This page ignores the date filter.
lt.compare.title: Why is this number different from the Overview?
lt.compare.html:
Overview (All) = {tx} is computed by this app from the {files} transcript files still on disk, which cover {firstTx} → {lastTx}.

Lifetime = {lt} is Claude Code's own running total since your first session on {first}. It still includes the {lostDays} days ({first} → {beforeTx}) whose transcripts Claude Code has deleted (it removes transcripts older than {days} days).

So the difference of {diff} is mostly the work from those deleted days. Small residual differences: the stats cache is refreshed by Claude Code only now and then (last on {computed}), it does not distinguish 1-hour from 5-minute cache writes, and it counts sessions from every device that syncs this folder.

From now on this app archives what it has parsed, so nothing more gets lost; set "cleanupPeriodDays": 365 in settings.json to keep the raw files too.

help.title: Glossary — how to read the numbers
help.intro:
The one mental model

Claude Code talks to a stateless API. For every step it sends the entire conversation so far — system prompt, CLAUDE.md, every message, every tool result — and gets one response back. A single prompt you type typically turns into many such calls:

you: "fix the failing test"
  call 1  → model reads the test file        (Read)         ctx  60k
  call 2  → runs the tests                   (Bash)         ctx  72k   ← test output now in context
  call 3  → reads the implementation         (Read)         ctx  80k
  call 4  → edits it                         (Edit)         ctx  86k
  call 5  → runs the tests again             (Bash)         ctx  94k
  call 6  → "Done, the test passes"                         ctx  98k

Each call is billed for its whole context: the part that was already sent before is a cache read (cheap per token, but it is 95%+ of all tokens), the new part is a cache write, and the answer is output. So the price of a session ≈ Σ over calls of (context size). That is why long sessions and big tool results dominate the bill, not the number of prompts you type.
help.attribution:
How the attribution works ("Where tokens go")

For each call the app knows from the API how many new tokens entered the context (cache write + uncached input) and what arrived since the previous call: the model's own answer, the results of the tools it used (linked by tool_use_id), the instructions of a skill it invoked, subagent hand-backs, your prompt, and system reminders. The new tokens are split between those items in proportion to their character length. Each item then gets an ingest cost (cache write) and a carry cost (it is re-read on every later call until a compaction resets the context — detected as a sharp drop in context size). Output tokens of a call go to the tool that call decided to use. Subagent transcripts are separate conversations; their full cost is shown as "Subagent run: <type>". The sum of all buckets matches the total to within a few percent.

Where the data comes from

  • ~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session>.jsonl — the transcript; every assistant line carries the API usage block (one line per content block, de-duplicated by message.id).
  • <session>/subagents/**/agent-*.jsonl (+ .meta.json) — subagent and workflow-agent transcripts.
  • ~/.claude/stats-cache.json — Claude Code's own lifetime counters (Lifetime page).
  • ~/.claude/settings.json, .last-cleanup — retention settings.
  • Other things in ~/.claude that this app does not use: history.jsonl (your prompt history per project), file-history/ (file checkpoints for /rewind), plans/ (plan-mode plans), shell-snapshots/, skills/ and plugins/ (installed skills), projects/*/memory/ (auto-memory).
gloss.cost: Estimated from token counts × list price (src/lib/pricing.ts). On a subscription plan (Pro/Max) this is what the same work would cost on the API — useful as a relative measure of what eats your plan limits.
gloss.reported: totalCostUSD from the last cost-state record Claude Code wrote into the transcript. Only some sessions have it, and a resumed session carries the previous session's total forward, so it can over-count.
gloss.apicalls: One API call = one request to the model. Every assistant turn (text, thinking, or a tool call) is one call. After each tool call Claude Code sends the whole conversation again for the next step, so one prompt usually becomes many calls.
gloss.toolcalls: Number of tool invocations (Bash, Read, Edit, MCP tools, subagents…) inside the API calls. One call can contain several tool uses.
gloss.prompts: Messages you actually typed or pasted (system-injected messages, tool results and subagent hand-backs are excluded).
gloss.output: Tokens the model generated: visible text, thinking, and tool inputs (e.g. the content of a file it writes). Billed at the output rate — the most expensive token type.
gloss.cacheread: Tokens re-read from the prompt cache. Because the whole conversation is re-sent on every call, this is by far the largest token count. Billed at ~10% of the input rate — but with thousands of calls it is usually the biggest cost line.
gloss.cachewrite: Tokens written into the prompt cache for the first time: new content that entered the context on that call (tool results, your prompt, the previous answer). 5m TTL costs 1.25× input, 1h TTL 2×.
gloss.input: Uncached input tokens billed at the full input rate. Normally tiny because Claude Code caches nearly everything.
gloss.apitime: Sum of the time the model spent answering (turn durations reported by Claude Code). Wall time is the span from first to last message of a session.
gloss.ctx: Context size = everything sent to the model on one call (system prompt + conversation + tool results). Average over the session's calls. Bigger context ⇒ every call costs more.
gloss.startup: Tokens present before you typed anything: system prompt, tool definitions, CLAUDE.md, MCP server instructions, skill listing. Paid again (as cache read) on every call of the session.
gloss.misses: Calls where the cache could not be used and the whole context was re-processed at the cache-write rate: after an idle break longer than the cache TTL (1h on a subscription, 5m on API/usage credits), a model or effort switch, or an upgrade.
gloss.carry: Carry cost: once content is in the context it is re-read (cache read) on every later call until the context is compacted or cleared. A 20k-token file read early in a 500-call session costs 20k × 500 cache reads.
gloss.ingest: Ingest cost: the cache-write cost of putting content into the context the first time.
gloss.outcost: Output cost of the calls that decided to use this tool (the model's text/thinking/tool input for that step).
gloss.think: Thinking tokens (extended reasoning), part of output tokens. Controlled by the effort level (/effort) — lower effort spends fewer of them.
gloss.subagents: Subagent transcripts (<session>/subagents/*.jsonl) run in their own context; their calls and cost are attributed to the parent session.
gloss.lifetime: Claude Code's own running counters since your first session, including days whose transcripts were deleted. See the explanation box on this page for why it differs from the Overview.

settings.title: Claude Code settings
settings.lead: These keys in your settings.json change what this dashboard can measure. Editing them here writes the file for you (a timestamped backup is kept next to it); every other key is preserved.
settings.readonly: The settings file is not writable from here — the changes below will fail.
settings.restart: Takes effect in sessions you start after the change.
settings.retentionHint: How long Claude Code keeps transcripts before deleting them. Raise it to keep your history (this dashboard archives what it already parsed, but only raw files can be re-analysed).
settings.ttlHint: Prompt-cache lifetime of the main conversation. 1h keeps the cache warm through longer breaks (cache writes cost 2× instead of 1.25×, a rebuild costs far more). Default: 1h on a subscription, 5m on an API key.
settings.subTtlHint: Prompt-cache lifetime of subagents, workflows and compaction. Default is 5m everywhere.
gloss.retention: cleanupPeriodDays in ~/.claude/settings.json: Claude Code deletes transcripts older than this at startup (30 days by default). This dashboard keeps parsed data of deleted transcripts in its own cache, but raising the value keeps the raw files too.
settings.page.title: Settings
settings.page.lead: Everything this dashboard can change or needs to know about: the Claude Code keys that decide what can be measured, how the app looks, where it reads from, and the prices it calculates with.

prices.builtinUpdated: checked against Anthropic's pricing page on {date}
prices.how: Prices ship with the app, so it works offline and every figure is reproducible. Refreshing downloads a public, machine-readable price list (a plain GET — nothing about you is sent), stores it in cache/prices.json and recomputes every cost. You can also just edit src/lib/pricing.ts.
prices.differsHint: differs from the price built into the app
gloss.prices: Every cost on this dashboard is token count × these list prices — Claude Code's transcripts contain no dollar amounts. The table ships with the app; you can refresh it from a public price list or edit src/lib/pricing.ts. Changing it recomputes every session immediately, so old numbers change too.
